concepts.title: The Group Axioms
concepts.contentHtml:
A group is a set with an operation that satisfies four rules:

1. Closure: combining two elements gives another element in the set
2. Associativity: (a • b) • c = a • (b • c)
3. Identity: there's an element e where a • e = e • a = a
4. Inverses: every element a has an a⁻¹ where a • a⁻¹ = e

Groups capture the essence of symmetry — the ways you can transform something and still have it look the same.
mathExpressions: (G, \cdot) \text{ with } e \in G, \; a^{-1} \in G \; \forall a

concepts.title: Examples of Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
(ℤ, +): Integers under addition. Identity = 0. Inverse of 5 is -5.

(ℤ/nℤ, +): Integers mod n. This is "clock arithmetic" — it's a group!

Symmetries of a square: 4 rotations + 4 reflections = 8 elements. This is the dihedral group D₄.

Non-example: Natural numbers under addition. No inverses (can't have -3 in ℕ), so not a group.

concepts.title: Abelian vs Non-Abelian
concepts.contentHtml:
A group is abelian (commutative) if a • b = b • a for all elements.

(ℤ, +) is abelian: 3 + 5 = 5 + 3. ✓

The symmetries of a square are non-abelian: rotating then reflecting is different from reflecting then rotating!

Non-commutativity is the source of much of group theory's richness and difficulty. It's also why matrix multiplication is non-commutative — matrices form a group (GLₙ).

title: Subgroups & Cyclic Groups
description: Groups within groups and the power of generators

concepts.title: Subgroups
concepts.contentHtml:
A subgroup H of G is a subset that is itself a group under the same operation.

The even integers are a subgroup of (ℤ, +). The rotations of a square are a subgroup of D₄.

Lagrange's Theorem: The size of a subgroup always divides the size of the group. If |G| = 12, subgroups can only have size 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, or 12.

This dramatically limits what subgroups can exist!

concepts.title: Cyclic Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
A cyclic group is generated by a single element — every element is a power of that generator.

ℤ/6ℤ is cyclic: generated by 1 (or by 5). Every element is a sum of 1's.

The rotations of an n-gon form a cyclic group of order n: one rotation generates all others.

Every group of prime order is cyclic. This is a direct consequence of Lagrange's theorem!

concepts.title: Cosets & Quotient Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
A coset of H in G is a "shifted copy" of H: gH = {gh : h ∈ H}.

Cosets partition the group into equal-sized pieces. The number of cosets is |G|/|H| — this is why Lagrange's theorem works.

If H is a normal subgroup (gHg⁻¹ = H for all g), the cosets themselves form a group called the quotient group G/H. This is how you "divide" groups.

concepts.title: The Symmetric Group Sₙ
concepts.contentHtml:
The symmetric group Sₙ is the group of all permutations (rearrangements) of n objects.

S₃ has 3! = 6 elements. S₄ has 4! = 24 elements. Sₙ has n! elements.

Cayley's Theorem: Every group is isomorphic to a subgroup of some Sₙ. This means permutation groups are universal — they contain every possible group structure!

concepts.title: Cycle Notation
concepts.contentHtml:
Cycle notation is a compact way to write permutations.

(1 3 2) means: 1→3, 3→2, 2→1. It's a 3-cycle.

Every permutation decomposes uniquely into disjoint cycles. (1 3)(2 4) means: swap 1↔3 and swap 2↔4 simultaneously.

Transpositions are 2-cycles like (1 2). Every permutation can be written as a product of transpositions.

concepts.title: Even & Odd Permutations
concepts.contentHtml:
A permutation is even if it's a product of an even number of transpositions, and odd otherwise.

The alternating group Aₙ consists of all even permutations. It has n!/2 elements and is always a normal subgroup of Sₙ.

A₅ is the smallest non-abelian simple group (no normal subgroups except {e} and itself). This is why there's no general formula for roots of polynomials of degree ≥ 5 (Abel-Ruffini theorem)!

concepts.title: Group Homomorphisms
concepts.contentHtml:
A homomorphism is a function between groups that preserves the operation: f(ab) = f(a)f(b).

Example: det: GLₙ → ℝ* sends matrices to their determinants. det(AB) = det(A)·det(B). ✓

The kernel of a homomorphism is the set mapped to the identity. It's always a normal subgroup. For det, the kernel is SLₙ (matrices with determinant 1).

The First Isomorphism Theorem: G/ker(f) ≅ im(f). Quotient out what's collapsed, and you get the image.

concepts.title: Symmetry in Physics
concepts.contentHtml:
Noether's Theorem: Every continuous symmetry of a physical system corresponds to a conserved quantity.

• Translational symmetry ↔ Conservation of momentum
• Rotational symmetry ↔ Conservation of angular momentum
• Time symmetry ↔ Conservation of energy

The Standard Model of particle physics is built on the symmetry group SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1). Different particles are representations of this group.

concepts.title: Groups in Chemistry, Music, and More
concepts.contentHtml:
Chemistry: Molecular symmetry groups predict which spectral transitions are allowed, which molecules are chiral, and how crystals form. The 230 crystallographic space groups classify all possible crystal structures.

Music theory: The twelve musical notes form ℤ/12ℤ. Transposition and inversion are group operations. Twelve-tone serialism is group theory applied to composition.

Rubik's Cube: The moves form a group with 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 elements. Group theory proved it can always be solved in ≤20 moves.

title: Group Actions
description: Groups acting on sets, orbits, and counting with symmetry

concepts.title: Groups Acting on Sets
concepts.contentHtml:
A group action is a way for a group G to "move around" the elements of a set X. Formally, it's a map G × X → X satisfying two rules:

1. The identity does nothing: e • x = x
2. Actions compose: (gh) • x = g • (h • x)

Examples are everywhere: rotations act on points of a polygon, Sₙ acts on {1, 2, ..., n} by permuting elements, and GLₙ acts on ℝⁿ by matrix multiplication.

Group actions unify seemingly unrelated problems by revealing them as different instances of the same algebraic structure acting on different sets.
mathExpressions: G \times X \to X, \quad e \cdot x = x, \quad (gh) \cdot x = g \cdot (h \cdot x)

concepts.title: Orbits and Stabilizers
concepts.contentHtml:
When a group acts on a set, each element x has two important associated structures:

The orbit of x, Orb(x), is the set of all elements that x can be moved to: {g • x : g ∈ G}.

The stabilizer of x, Stab(x), is the set of group elements that fix x: {g ∈ G : g • x = x}. The stabilizer is always a subgroup of G.

Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem: |G| = |Orb(x)| × |Stab(x)|. The group's size equals the orbit size times the stabilizer size. This connects the "geometry" (orbits) to the "algebra" (subgroups).

concepts.title: Burnside's Counting Lemma
concepts.contentHtml:
Burnside's Lemma (also called the Cauchy-Frobenius lemma) counts distinct objects under symmetry:

Number of distinct objects = (1/|G|) × Σ |Fix(g)|, where Fix(g) is the number of elements fixed by each group element g.

Classic example: How many distinct necklaces can you make with 4 beads of 2 colors? Without symmetry: 2⁴ = 16 colorings. But the rotation group has 4 elements. Burnside says: (1/4)(16 + 2 + 4 + 2) = 6 distinct necklaces.

This technique is essential in chemistry (counting distinct molecular configurations), combinatorics, and even music theory.

title: Sylow Theorems
description: The deep structure of finite groups

concepts.title: p-Groups and Sylow p-Subgroups
concepts.contentHtml:
A p-group is a group whose order is a power of a prime p. For example, ℤ/4ℤ and ℤ/2ℤ × ℤ/2ℤ are both 2-groups (order 4 = 2²).

Given any finite group G of order n, write n = pᵏ × m where p does not divide m. A Sylow p-subgroup is a subgroup of G having order exactly pᵏ — the maximum possible power of p.

Sylow subgroups are the "prime building blocks" of finite groups. Understanding them is the key to understanding the full group's structure.

concepts.title: The Three Sylow Theorems
concepts.contentHtml:
The three Sylow theorems are cornerstones of finite group theory:

Sylow I (Existence): For every prime power pᵏ dividing |G|, there exists a subgroup of order pᵏ. In particular, Sylow p-subgroups always exist.

Sylow II (Conjugacy): All Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate to each other. They're all "the same" up to relabeling by the group.

Sylow III (Counting): The number nₚ of Sylow p-subgroups satisfies nₚ ≡ 1 (mod p) and nₚ divides |G|/pᵏ. This severely restricts the possibilities.

concepts.title: Classifying Groups of Small Order
concepts.contentHtml:
The Sylow theorems are a powerful tool for classifying groups. Here's how they work in practice:

Order 15: |G| = 3 × 5. Sylow III gives n₃ | 5 and n₃ ≡ 1 (mod 3), so n₃ = 1. Similarly n₅ = 1. Both Sylow subgroups are normal, so G ≅ ℤ₁₅. There's only one group of order 15!

Order 12: |G| = 2² × 3. More complex: n₃ ∈ {1, 4}. If n₃ = 1, the Sylow 3-subgroup is normal. This yields 5 possible groups, including ℤ₁₂, D₆, A₄, and others.

This approach systematically reveals the "periodic table" of finite groups.

title: Rings & Fields
description: Beyond groups: algebraic structures with two operations

concepts.title: Rings: Two Operations at Once
concepts.contentHtml:
A ring is a set with two operations (addition and multiplication) where:

1. (R, +) is an abelian group
2. Multiplication is associative and distributes over addition
3. There's a multiplicative identity 1 (in a ring with unity)

Examples: The integers ℤ, polynomial rings ℤ[x], matrices Mₙ(ℝ), and clock arithmetic ℤ/nℤ are all rings.

Non-example nuance: Matrices are a ring, but multiplication isn't commutative. ℤ is a ring, but most elements lack multiplicative inverses. These "failures" lead to rich theory.
mathExpressions: a(b + c) = ab + ac, \quad (a + b)c = ac + bc

concepts.title: Ideals and Quotient Rings
concepts.contentHtml:
An ideal I of a ring R is like a normal subgroup, but for rings: it absorbs multiplication. For any r ∈ R and a ∈ I, both ra and ar belong to I.

The quotient ring R/I consists of cosets and inherits a natural ring structure. This is how we "mod out" by an ideal.

Key example: In ℤ, the even integers 2ℤ form an ideal. ℤ/2ℤ = {0, 1} is the ring of integers mod 2 (a field!).

In ℝ[x], the ideal (x² + 1) gives ℝ[x]/(x² + 1) ≅ ℂ — the complex numbers arise as a quotient ring! This is a profound connection.

concepts.title: Fields and Their Extensions
concepts.contentHtml:
A field is a ring where every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. Fields are where you can add, subtract, multiply, and divide.

Examples: ℚ, ℝ, ℂ, and the finite fields 𝔽ₚ = ℤ/pℤ (for p prime). The rationals are the smallest field containing the integers.

Finite fields are remarkable: there is exactly one field of order pⁿ for each prime power, denoted 𝔽_{p^n} or GF(pⁿ). These are the backbone of coding theory, cryptography (AES uses 𝔽_{2^8}), and algebraic geometry over finite fields.

Field extensions: ℚ ⊂ ℚ(√2) ⊂ ℝ ⊂ ℂ. Each step "adds" new elements. Understanding these extensions is the gateway to Galois theory.

title: Galois Theory Intro
description: Symmetries of equations and the fate of the quintic

concepts.title: Field Extensions and Splitting Fields
concepts.contentHtml:
Given a polynomial, its splitting field is the smallest field containing all its roots.

For x² - 2 over ℚ, the roots are ±√2, so the splitting field is ℚ(√2). The degree of this extension is [ℚ(√2) : ℚ] = 2.

For x³ - 2 over ℚ, the splitting field is ℚ(³√2, ω) where ω = e^{2πi/3} is a primitive cube root of unity. This extension has degree 6.

The Galois group of an extension is the group of all field automorphisms that fix the base field. It captures the symmetries of the roots.

concepts.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory establishes a perfect correspondence between:

• Intermediate fields between the base field and the splitting field
• Subgroups of the Galois group

Bigger subgroups correspond to smaller intermediate fields (the correspondence is order-reversing).

Normal subgroups correspond to normal extensions (Galois extensions). This transforms field-theoretic questions into group-theoretic ones — and groups are often easier to work with!

This is one of the most beautiful results in all of mathematics: it bridges algebra (groups) with geometry (field extensions) in a perfect bijection.
mathExpressions: \{\text{subgroups of Gal}(E/F)\} \longleftrightarrow \{\text{intermediate fields } F \subseteq K \subseteq E\}

concepts.title: Why There's No Quintic Formula
concepts.contentHtml:
There are formulas for roots of polynomials of degree 2 (quadratic formula), 3 (Cardano's), and 4 (Ferrari's). For centuries, mathematicians sought a degree 5 formula.

Abel and Galois proved it doesn't exist. Here's the key insight:

A polynomial is solvable by radicals iff its Galois group is a solvable group (one that can be broken down through abelian quotients). The generic quintic has Galois group S₅.

S₅ is NOT solvable because A₅ is simple and non-abelian — it can't be broken into abelian pieces. Therefore, no formula using only +, -, ×, ÷, and radicals can solve the general quintic.

Évariste Galois discovered this at age 20, the night before he died in a duel. His work founded an entire branch of mathematics and remains central to modern algebra.
mathExpressions: S_5 \supset A_5 \supset \{e\}, \quad A_5 \text{ simple } \Rightarrow S_5 \text{ not solvable}
